title: Albanese plunges into AI copyright fight amid claims of ‘stitch-up’
source_used: AFR (opening paragraph only, paywalled); ABC News for the inquiry and the stitch-up row
key_facts: AFR: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says global AI labs are already using the works of Australia's creatives to train AI models without payment or consent and that changes to copyright laws are about taking control of the situation.

AFR: on Tuesday (13 Oct 2026) he gave his strongest comments so far supporting copyright changes, after a bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into AI gave the green light to press ahead with changes that would make it easier for developers to train models in local data centres.

ABC News: the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence recommended independent safety checks on AI companies, reserving computing power for local use, early access to new models for security agencies, investment in data centres with national standards, and a review of Australia's copyright settings.
ABC News: the copyright review would be at odds with creative groups that want stronger enforcement of existing protections; the final report is due in November.

ABC News: independent Senator David Pocock said an adviser to Albanese 'pre-vetted' the committee's early advice letter and raised 'mark-ups' from the prime minister's office; he said 'We've seen enough major party stitch ups'.
ABC News: committee chair Jo Briskey (Labor) and deputy chair Senator Jonno Duniam (Liberal) denied interference; Duniam said 'There has been no guidance, no interference'.
ABC News: the government hopes to introduce legislation on national standards for data centres and frontier AI models by the end of this year and pass it in early 2027.
quote_evidence: Albanese on Tuesday gave his strongest comments to date supporting changes to copyright laws, after a bipartisan parliamentary inquiry into AI gave the green light to press ahead with changes that would make it easier for developers to train their models in local data centres.
Labor and the Coalition have denied there was "interference" in a raft of recommendations from an artificial intelligence inquiry after accusations of a major party "stitch-up".
why_it_matters_hint: Australia's prime minister has publicly backed changing copyright law over AI training, while a senator alleges the prime minister's office interfered in the inquiry's advice.
notes: AFR article is behind a subscription; only its opening paragraph was available. The inquiry and the row were read in ABC News (https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-13/ai-inquiry-independent-safety-watchdogs/107258612). Details of what Albanese said beyond the AFR opening are not known.
